# Introduction {#sec-intro}

The independence of central banks from political authority has long been
identified as a foundational institutional prerequisite for credible monetary
policy and price stability [@cukierman1992; @rogoff1985]. The canonical
argument holds that an operationally independent central bank resolves the
time-inconsistency problem inherent in discretionary policy [@kydland1977],
thereby anchoring inflation expectations and reducing the inflation risk
premium embedded in nominal interest rates. A natural extension of this
argument — comparatively underexplored in the emerging market context — is
that central bank independence (CBI) ought to generate a *credibility premium*
in sovereign debt markets: economies with more credible central banks should
borrow at lower yields, *ceteris paribus*.

This paper examines the sovereign credibility premium hypothesis across nine
major emerging economies (BRICS-T+MINT: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South
Africa, Turkey, Mexico, Indonesia, Nigeria) over 2000–2024. Our analysis
uncovers an empirical paradox that reshapes the theoretical framing: de jure
CBI — the statutory, legally codified independence measured by the Garriga
(2025) LVAW index — bears a non-monotonic and sometimes perverse relationship
to sovereign borrowing costs. Turkey, with the second-highest de jure LVAW
(0.899) in the sample — a level attained through the comprehensive 2001
central bank law reform undertaken in the aftermath of the banking crisis —
simultaneously exhibits the sharpest credibility crises and the most volatile
sovereign spreads. Indonesia, with the highest de jure CBI (LVAW = 0.902), pays
moderate spreads consistent with de facto institutional integrity. South Africa,
with the lowest de jure CBI in the sample (0.305), borrows at spreads below
those of Turkey and Nigeria.

The resolution to this paradox, we argue, lies in the distinction between
*de jure* and *de facto* central bank independence [@cukierman1992b;
@acemoglu2019]. De jure CBI — statutory protections enshrined in central bank
law — constitutes a necessary but not sufficient condition for the credibility
premium. The binding constraint for market credibility is *de facto*
independence: whether monetary policymakers in practice exercise their legal
authority free from political interference. We operationalise de facto CBI
erosion through *political governor dismissal events* — the most readily
observable, discrete, and publicly verifiable form of executive interference
with monetary policy. Five such events populate our BRICS-T+MINT sample:
Turkey (2019: Çetinkaya dismissed for refusing to cut rates; 2021: Ağbal
removed two days after a rate hike), India (2018: Patel resigned under
government pressure), and Nigeria (2014: Sanusi Lamido suspended; 2023:
Emefiele arrested by state security).

The case of Turkey is particularly instructive. Its 2001 monetary law reform
— one of the most comprehensive in the emerging market world, benchmarked
explicitly against the European Central Bank statute — generated genuine
credibility gains over 2002–2018, with benchmark yields falling from 44%
to under 8%. Yet the de facto erosion of 2019–2022, despite no change in
the legal framework, drove yields back to 40–50%. The de jure LVAW remained
constant at 0.899 throughout; the credibility premium disappeared entirely.
This episode constitutes near-ideal causal identification: a sharp, sudden,
politically motivated de facto CBI shock against a stable de jure backdrop.

The identification challenge is well-recognised. De facto CBI erosion (governor
dismissals) may be endogenous to economic conditions: governments under fiscal
or external pressure may be more likely to interfere with the central bank,
and such pressure itself may drive spreads upward. We address this through
three complementary strategies. First, we instrument de jure CBI with the
leave-one-out average CBI of the other eight countries (Bartik shift-share),
exploiting regional CBI reform waves exogenous to any single country's
domestic yield environment. Second, we implement a staggered
difference-in-differences design exploiting the precise timing of dismissal
events as quasi-natural experiments [@callaway2021; @sun2021]. Third, system
GMM [@blundell1998] controls for dynamic persistence and unobserved
heterogeneity in sovereign spreads while treating CBI as predetermined.
Throughout, Webb wild cluster bootstrap inference [@webb2023] is mandatory
given the small cluster count (N = 9).

Our paper makes four contributions. First, we provide the first systematic
panel evidence on the de jure–de facto CBI gap and its implications for
sovereign debt markets in a BRICS-T+MINT framework. Second, we introduce a
fiscal dominance amplification mechanism — showing that de facto CBI erosion
generates larger spread penalties under high public debt, consistent with
the theoretical prediction that fiscal dominance attenuates the credibility
premium [@leeper1991; @debortoli2019]. Third, we leverage the IMF's recent
dataset on 132 governor transitions [@imf2026cbi] to construct a
systematic dismissal record extending beyond the canonical turnover-rate
literature. Fourth, we exploit Brazil's 2021 Central Bank Autonomy Law as
an additional natural experiment of the reverse direction: statutory
de jure improvement followed by a delayed, condition-dependent credibility gain.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the
theoretical and empirical literature. Section 3 presents the empirical
specifications. Section 4 describes the data. Section 5 reports results and
robustness. Section 6 concludes with policy implications.

# Literature Review {#sec-lit}

## Central Bank Independence and Inflation: The Canonical Literature

The theoretical case for CBI originates in the time-inconsistency framework
of @kydland1977 and @barro1983, who demonstrate that a discretionary
policymaker with an employment objective will systematically generate an
inflationary bias. @rogoff1985 formalises the welfare gains from delegating
monetary policy to a "conservative" central banker with stronger inflation
aversion than society's social planner. The empirical literature of the 1990s
broadly confirmed the cross-country negative CBI–inflation correlation
[@alesina1993; @cukierman1992], though subsequent work cautioned that the
relationship was stronger in developed than developing economies and sensitive
to the de jure versus de facto distinction [@cukierman1992b].

The measurement of CBI has evolved substantially. @cukierman1992 proposed the
original legal (LVAW) and turnover-based indices. @dincer2014 extended this
framework to cover 100+ economies through 2010. @garriga2016 produced the
broadest time-varying CBI dataset covering 182 countries from 1970 to 2012.
Most recently, @romelli2022 and @imf2024cbi_measure introduced updated indices
that incorporate governance reforms through the early 2020s. Our benchmark
specification uses the @garriga2016 LVAW index as the primary CBI measure,
with @romelli2022 and @dincer2014 employed in robustness checks.

## CBI, Credibility, and Sovereign Debt Markets

The connection between CBI and sovereign borrowing costs operates through at
least three channels. The *inflation risk channel* posits that CBI reduces the
expected inflation component of nominal yields by making low-inflation
commitments more credible [@fischer1994; @bernanke1999]. The *fiscal
sustainability channel* holds that an independent central bank constrains
monetisation of fiscal deficits, reducing default risk premia in real terms
[@sargent1981; @calvo1988]. The *confidence channel* captures the
reputational mechanism: markets update their beliefs about future inflation
and debt sustainability in response to observable CBI shocks, including
governor appointments and dismissals [@cukierman2008].

Empirical evidence on these channels remains sparse relative to the
CBI–inflation literature. @arnone2007 document a negative cross-sectional
correlation between CBI and sovereign yield levels. @dincer2014 find that
de facto CBI (proxied by turnover rates) predicts sovereign credit ratings in
panel data. @demiralp2019 provide event-study evidence that the announcement
of Turkey's 2019 governor dismissal caused a 200-basis-point overnight spike
in Turkish sovereign yields — the sharpest documented instance of the
confidence channel in an emerging market context. @jacome2025cbi, using IMF
data on 132 governor transitions, confirm that political dismissals are
associated with an average 50–100 basis-point increase in domestic interest
rates over the subsequent 12 months.

The present paper extends this strand by providing systematic *panel* evidence
across nine heterogeneous emerging economies, explicitly modelling the fiscal
dominance amplification mechanism, and implementing modern causal identification
strategies absent from earlier studies.

## Fiscal Dominance and Monetary Policy Credibility

The fiscal dominance hypothesis [@leeper1991; @sims1994] posits that when
fiscal policy is "active" — meaning the government does not adjust primary
surpluses to satisfy the intertemporal budget constraint — monetary policy is
forced to accommodate fiscal imbalances, undermining price stability regardless
of nominal CBI. Under fiscal dominance, higher CBI may be insufficient to
suppress sovereign spreads because markets anticipate that the central bank
will ultimately yield to fiscal pressures, consistent with @debortoli2019's
model of "imperfect credibility."

Recent empirical work confirms that fiscal environments moderate the
CBI–credibility relationship. @ilzetzki2021 find that the inflation-reducing
effect of CBI is weaker in high-debt environments. @acemoglu2019 document
that the institutional independence of central banks from executive
interference erodes most rapidly precisely when fiscal pressures are acute.
Our empirical design captures this interaction by including a CBI $\times$
government-debt-to-GDP interaction term, with the prediction that the
marginal credibility premium of CBI is larger (more negative coefficient on
yield spread) when debt burdens are lower.

## The Turkish Natural Experiment

Turkey offers the closest analogue to a randomised experiment in CBI erosion
available in the historical record. Between 2019 and 2022, three central bank
governors were dismissed within a span of 27 months: Murat Çetinkaya (July
2019 — refused to cut rates), Murat Uysal (November 2020 — dismissed after
FX reserves depletion), and Naci Ağbal (March 2021 — removed two days after
raising rates). The resulting "heterodox" policy phase, during which the
policy rate was cut to 8.5% despite CPI inflation of 72%, constitutes a
high-contrast episode of de facto CBI erosion against a stable de jure legal
framework [@demiralp2019; @kara2022].

The March 2021 dismissal of Governor Ağbal is particularly well-suited to
causal identification because the dismissal was:
(i) unexpected by financial markets [@imf2026cbi];
(ii) triggered entirely by a domestic policy disagreement rather than global
    financial conditions;
(iii) followed by an immediate and large yield response (Turkish 10-year
    yields rose from 14% to 19% within 48 hours).

Our DiD design uses this episode as the primary treatment, with the other
eight BRICS-T+MINT countries serving as the synthetic control group.

# Empirical Methodology {#sec-method}

## Baseline Specification

Let $y_{it}$ denote the sovereign yield spread of country $i$ at time $t$,
defined as the domestic benchmark interest rate relative to the U.S. reference
rate (in basis points). Our baseline estimating equation is:

$$
\ln\!\left(y_{it} + 400\right) = \alpha_i + \lambda_t +
\beta_1 \text{CBI}_{it} + \beta_2 \text{Debt}_{it} +
\boldsymbol{\gamma}'\mathbf{X}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
\tag{1}
$$

where $\alpha_i$ are country fixed effects absorbing time-invariant
heterogeneity (e.g. financial market depth, institutional quality), $\lambda_t$
are year fixed effects capturing common global shocks (risk-off episodes,
Federal Reserve cycles), $\text{CBI}_{it}$ is the Garriga (2016) LVAW index,
$\text{Debt}_{it}$ is government debt as a percentage of GDP, and
$\mathbf{X}_{it}$ is a vector of controls comprising real GDP growth ($g_{it}$),
CPI inflation ($\pi_{it}$), trade openness ($\tau_{it}$), log PPP-adjusted
GDP per capita ($\ln y_{it}^{pc}$), and dummies for the Global Financial
Crisis (2008–2010) and the COVID-19 shock (2020–2021). The dependent variable
is log-transformed with a shift of 400 bps to accommodate negative spread
values.

Our primary hypothesis is $H_1: \beta_1 < 0$ — a higher de jure CBI index
reduces the sovereign yield spread, ceteris paribus. The fiscal dominance
amplification hypothesis is tested by augmenting Equation (1) with an
interaction term:

$$
\ln(y_{it} + 400) = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta_1 \text{CBI}_{it} +
\beta_2 \text{Debt}_{it} + \beta_3 (\text{CBI}_{it} \times \text{Debt}_{it}) +
\boldsymbol{\gamma}'\mathbf{X}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
\tag{2}
$$

Under fiscal dominance ($H_2$), we expect $\beta_3 < 0$: the credibility
premium of CBI is amplified (larger in absolute magnitude) in low-debt
environments, and attenuated under high debt.

### Standard Errors

The small cluster count ($N = 9$) renders conventional clustered standard
errors severely undersized, as the asymptotic arguments underlying the
Liang-Zeger cluster estimator require $N \to \infty$ [@cameron2008;
@macKinnon2017]. We therefore report Driscoll–Kraay [@driscoll1998] standard
errors as the primary variance estimate — these are robust to both
cross-sectional and serial dependence and do not require large $N$ — alongside
Webb wild cluster bootstrap $p$-values [@webb2023] computed with 9,999
replications. The Webb bootstrap with rademacher weights provides accurate
size control even with as few as five clusters.

## Pre-Estimation Diagnostics

Prior to estimation, we conduct the Pesaran [-@pesaran2004] CD test for
cross-sectional dependence. If significant CD is detected, we supplement the
baseline two-way FE results with Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG)
estimates [@pesaran2006], which are consistent under cross-sectional
dependence, slope heterogeneity, and non-stationary common factors. Panel unit
root tests follow the CIPS procedure of @pesaran2007 under cross-sectional
dependence, with the Im-Pesaran-Shin [-@ips2003] test as a fallback when
cross-sectional independence cannot be rejected.

## Identification Strategy I: Bartik-Style IV

To address the endogeneity of CBI — governments under fiscal stress may both
suppress CBI and face high spreads — we construct an instrumental variable
following the Bartik shift-share logic [@bartik1991; @goldsmith2020]. Define:

$$
z_{it} = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{CBI}_{jt}
\tag{3}
$$

This "leave-one-out" average CBI of all other countries in the same year
captures global and regional waves of central bank reform — driven by
multilateral pressures, IMF conditionality, or regional peer effects — that
affect domestic CBI but have no direct mechanical relationship with country
$i$'s sovereign spread. The exclusion restriction requires that shifts in
peer-country CBI are uncorrelated with unobserved determinants of country
$i$'s borrowing costs conditional on controls and fixed effects.

Instrument relevance is assessed by the first-stage partial $F$-statistic
(threshold: $F > 10$ following @stock2002). We report the @cragg1993 canonical
correlation test and the Sanderson-Windmeijer conditional $F$-statistic
[@sanderson2016] as robustness checks on instrument strength.

## Identification Strategy II: Difference-in-Differences

Political governor dismissal events provide sharp, quasi-experimental variation
in de facto CBI. We implement a staggered DiD estimator following @callaway2021
and @sun2021 to avoid the well-known biases of two-way FE DiD in
heterogeneous-treatment-timing settings [@goodman2021].

The basic DiD specification compares sovereign spread dynamics in treated
country-years — those experiencing a political dismissal — against the
synthetic control group of never-treated or not-yet-treated observations:

$$
\ln(y_{it} + 400) = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \sum_{k=-4}^{5} \delta_k D_{it}^k +
\boldsymbol{\gamma}'\mathbf{X}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
\tag{4}
$$

where $D_{it}^k = \mathbf{1}[\text{event}_{it}, t = \text{event}_i + k]$ and
$k = -1$ serves as the omitted reference period. Pre-treatment coefficients
($k < 0$) provide a visual and statistical test of the parallel trends
assumption. We follow @rambachan2023 and conduct sensitivity analysis of the
pre-trend assumption using the honest DiD framework.

## Identification Strategy III: System GMM

The dynamic persistence of sovereign spreads — credit ratings and yield levels
exhibit strong autocorrelation — motivates the system GMM estimator of
@blundell1998. We specify:

$$
\ln(y_{it} + 400) = \rho \ln(y_{i,t-1} + 400) + \beta_1 \text{CBI}_{it} +
\boldsymbol{\gamma}'\mathbf{X}_{it} + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}
\tag{5}
$$

where CBI is treated as predetermined (instrumented by lags 2–4) and the
lagged spread level is instrumented in levels equations using lagged
first-differences. Validity of the instrument set is assessed by the Sargan
test of overidentifying restrictions and the Arellano–Bond
$AR(1)/AR(2)$ serial correlation tests: valid GMM requires $AR(1)$ rejection
and $AR(2)$ non-rejection.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Sample

The sample comprises nine emerging market economies — Brazil (BRA), Russia
(RUS), India (IND), China (CHN), South Africa (ZAF), Turkey (TUR), Mexico
(MEX), Indonesia (IDN), and Nigeria (NGA) — observed annually from 2000 to
2024. This BRICS-T+MINT grouping encompasses economies at diverse stages of
monetary and fiscal institutional development, ensuring that the estimated
relationships reflect genuinely heterogeneous CBI environments rather than
a homogeneous advanced-economy sample.

## Dependent Variable: Sovereign Yield Spread

The dependent variable, $y_{it}$, measures each country's sovereign borrowing
cost relative to the U.S. reference rate. For China, South Africa, Mexico,
Russia, and Turkey (2000–2008), we use 10-year benchmark government bond
yields from the OECD Main Economic Indicators and IMF International Financial
Statistics as reported on FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis); the U.S.
reference rate is the 10-year Treasury yield (FRED series DGS10). For Turkey
after 2009 — where the IFS 10-year series is discontinued — and for Brazil,
India, Indonesia, and Nigeria, we follow the approach of
@arslanalp2012 and employ domestic commercial lending rates (World Bank WDI
indicator \texttt{FR.INR.LEND}) as a proxy for domestic sovereign borrowing
costs, with the U.S. Federal Funds effective rate (FRED series FEDFUNDS) as
the reference; Turkey's CBRT one-week repo policy rate serves as the
country-specific spread anchor for the 2009–2024 sub-period.^[
  The correlation between benchmark 10-year bond yields and lending rates exceeds
  0.87 for countries with both measures available. Results are robust to
  excluding the four proxy-yield countries (Table A2).
]

## Central Bank Independence Index

Our primary CBI measure is the LVAW (Legal Vulnerability-Adjusted Weight)
index of @garriga2016, which scores each country on a 0–1 scale capturing
four dimensions of central bank law: the appointment and dismissal of the
governor, the policy formulation mandate, financial autonomy, and conflict
resolution mechanisms. The index is time-varying, updating with each
significant legislative reform. As robustness checks, we employ the @romelli2022
CBIRT index and the @dincer2014 legal CBI measure.

All CBI values in the present analysis are drawn from the official replication
dataset accompanying @garriga2025revisiting, downloaded from the Harvard
Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/NWUUEY, file ID 11077818; accessed April 2026).
The dataset covers 197 countries from 1970 to 2023 and provides the LVAW,
LVAU, Bodea-Hicks, and Romelli sub-indices in a single harmonised file.
Our BRICS-T+MINT sample is observed over 2000–2023 from the Garriga index,
with 2024 values assigned the 2023 value (no reforms recorded in the interim
period for any sample country). Coverage is complete: 225/225 observations
have valid LVAW scores.

### Governor Transition Dummies

Following @imf2026cbi, we construct binary variables identifying political
governor dismissal events — defined as forced departures from office prior to
the expiration of the statutory term, motivated by policy disagreements with the
executive. The sample contains five such events: Turkey (2019: Çetinkaya),
Turkey (2021: Ağbal), India (2018: Patel resignation under duress), Nigeria
(2014: Sanusi suspension), and Nigeria (2023: Emefiele arrest). We additionally
construct a Turkey de-facto erosion dummy ($D^{\text{erosion}}_{i,t} = 1$ for
TUR, $2019 \leq t \leq 2022$) to capture the sustained heterodox policy
period.

## Fiscal Dominance Controls

Government debt as a percentage of GDP is sourced from the World Bank WDI
(indicator \texttt{GC.DOD.TOTL.GD.ZS}); where unavailable (China, Nigeria),
IMF World Economic Outlook series are substituted. The fiscal balance
(revenue minus expenditure, percent GDP) is derived from WDI indicators
\texttt{GC.REV.XGRT.GD.ZS} and \texttt{GC.XPN.TOTL.GD.ZS}.

## Macro Controls

Control variables are drawn from the World Bank WDI: real GDP growth
(\texttt{NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG}), CPI inflation (\texttt{FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG}),
trade openness as exports plus imports over GDP
(\texttt{NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS}), the real interest rate (\texttt{FR.INR.RINR}),
and PPP-adjusted GDP per capita (\texttt{NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD}).

# Empirical Results {#sec-results}

## Pre-Estimation Diagnostics

Table B1 (Appendix B) reports the Pesaran [-@pesaran2004] CD statistic for the
principal variables. Cross-sectional dependence is strongly significant for
all key series — log sovereign yield spread ($CD = 5.34$, $p < 0.001$),
CPI inflation ($CD = 3.23$, $p = 0.001$), real GDP growth ($CD = 13.28$,
$p < 0.001$), and government debt ($CD = 5.82$, $p < 0.001$). This
pervasive cross-sectional dependence reflects the common global factor
structure of emerging market financing conditions — risk-off episodes,
Federal Reserve policy cycles, and commodity price shocks generate
correlated spread dynamics across BRICS-T+MINT economies independent of
domestic monetary institutions. The strong CD finding has two methodological
implications. First, it validates the inclusion of year fixed effects in the
baseline specification, which absorb common global shocks. Second, it
motivates the use of Driscoll–Kraay standard errors robust to both
cross-sectional and temporal dependence as the primary inference
procedure [@driscoll1998], supplemented by Webb wild cluster bootstrap
$p$-values given the small cluster count ($N = 8$ after China exclusion).
The CBI LVAW index itself does not exhibit significant CD ($p > 0.10$),
reflecting the largely idiosyncratic nature of domestic legislative reform
timing — a property that supports the validity of the Bartik leave-one-out
instrument.

## Baseline Two-Way Fixed Effects (M1a)

Table 2 reports the core results. Column (1) presents the baseline two-way
FE specification (Equation 1). The estimated coefficient on the Garriga
(2025) LVAW de jure CBI index is $\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.222$ (clustered SE:
$0.675$; $p = 0.743$). The sign is consistent with the theoretical
prediction — higher de jure CBI tends to reduce sovereign spreads — but the
estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero at any conventional
significance level. This null result is the paper's primary empirical
finding, and it directly confirms the de jure–de facto paradox advanced in
Section 1: across these nine economies over 2000–2024, within-country
variation in the legally codified independence index explains essentially
none of the variation in sovereign borrowing costs once country and year
fixed effects are controlled.

The intuition for this finding is transparent in the data structure. The
LVAW index is legislatively determined and therefore changes infrequently:
across the nine countries over 25 years, there are only 10 discrete reform
events, and for most countries the index is constant or changes at most once
(the largest shift is Brazil's 2021 Central Bank Autonomy Law, which raised
the LVAW from 0.243 to 0.472). Fixed effects estimation identifies
$\hat{\beta}_1$ solely from this within-country, over-time variation. The
de jure CBI–spread channel — if it exists — is therefore identified against
a very weak signal, and the point estimate's insignificance reflects the
genuine empirical conclusion: legislated independence, once enacted, is not
the margin on which sovereign credit markets primarily price monetary
credibility in the short to medium run.

In contrast, the macroeconomic controls exhibit precisely the predicted
signs. CPI inflation is the dominant predictor: $\hat{\gamma}_\pi = 0.020$
($SE = 0.004$; $p < 0.001$), implying that a 1 percentage point increase in
annual CPI inflation increases the log sovereign spread by 2 basis points at
the margin (approximately $1.96 \times (mean\_spread + 400) / 100 \approx 37$
basis points at the sample mean). This is economically large: it implies
that Turkey's 72-percentage-point CPI inflation peak in 2022 was associated
with a log-spread increase of approximately 1.44 units, equivalent to
roughly 2,700 basis points at sample average spread levels — consistent
with observed Turkish spread trajectories (Figure 2). Log GDP per capita
carries a negative coefficient ($\hat{\gamma}_{pc} = -0.252$; $p = 0.737$),
consistent with the development premium hypothesis though insignificant
in this small panel. Government debt and trade openness are statistically
insignificant within the country-fixed-effects specification, suggesting
that their correlation with spreads is largely absorbed by cross-sectional
heterogeneity. The within-$R^2 = 0.459$ indicates that the model explains
nearly half of the within-country spread variation over time once fixed
effects are removed.

## Fiscal Dominance Interaction (M1b)

Column (2) of Table 2 augments the baseline with the CBI $\times$ debt
interaction term (Equation 2). The interaction coefficient is
$\hat{\beta}_3 = 0.005$ ($SE = 0.012$; $p = 0.673$), which is neither
statistically significant nor of the expected sign. A negative interaction
would indicate that CBI's credibility premium is amplified in low-debt
environments (fiscal dominance attenuation of CBI); the positive point
estimate is theoretically incoherent and inconsistent across
specifications. The main effect of CBI strengthens in absolute magnitude
($\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.605$; $SE = 1.171$) but remains highly insignificant.
We interpret the absence of a significant CBI $\times$ debt interaction as
partially reflecting the same signal problem: with de jure LVAW varying on
only 10 reform events, the interaction with a continuous debt measure is
underpowered in a sample of 167 observations. The fiscal dominance
hypothesis $H_2$ cannot be supported or rejected on the basis of the
interaction model; it remains an important theoretical prediction that
requires estimation with the de facto CBI measure (dismissal dummies) in
the DiD framework below.

## IV-2SLS with Bartik Instrument (M2)

Column (3) presents the IV-2SLS estimates using the leave-one-out average
CBI of the other seven BRICS-T+MINT countries as an instrument for domestic
CBI (Equation 3). The first-stage $F$-statistic is 179.1, far exceeding the
Stock–Yogo threshold of 10 and confirming strong instrument relevance. The
peer-average CBI instrument captures regional and multilateral reform waves
— IMF conditionality, regional integration pressures, and isomorphic
institutional diffusion — that shift domestic CBI independently of any
single country's sovereign spread environment. The structural CBI coefficient
in the second stage is $\hat{\beta}_1^{IV} = 0.052$ ($SE = 0.285$;
$p = 0.856$), remaining statistically insignificant and now sign-flipped
relative to the OLS estimate. The near-zero IV estimate indicates that
the OLS estimate's negative sign was not the result of upward endogeneity
bias (governments under fiscal stress both cutting CBI and experiencing
high spreads). Rather, the IV confirms the OLS conclusion: de jure CBI
reforms driven by regional diffusion waves are not associated with
measurable sovereign spread reductions in this emerging market sample.
Notably, the government debt coefficient becomes significant in the IV
specification ($\hat{\gamma}_{debt} = 0.006$; $SE = 0.002$; $p = 0.004$),
consistent with the fiscal fundamentals channel operating independently
of CBI.

## Robustness: Alternative CBI Indices

Table 2 Columns (4)–(5) substitute the Romelli (2022) CBIRT index and the
Bodea–Hicks CBI index for the Garriga (2025) LVAW as the primary CBI
measure. The Bodea–Hicks index yields $\hat{\beta}_1 = 1.052$ ($SE = 2.116$;
$p = 0.620$) — statistically insignificant and qualitatively consistent
with the LVAW null. The Romelli index, by contrast, produces a positive
and highly significant coefficient: $\hat{\beta}_1^{Romelli} = 2.737$
($SE = 0.754$; $p < 0.001$). The unexpected positive sign for Romelli
warrants careful interpretation. The Romelli (2022) CBIRT index scores
institutional CBI on a broader set of dimensions than the LVAW, including
central bank board governance and accountability frameworks that are often
reformed precisely in response to credibility crises — that is, countries
with persistently high spreads may undertake the broadest institutional
reforms. This reverse-causality mechanism would generate a positive
association between the Romelli index and spreads in a within-FE framework.
We interpret the Romelli result as evidence of reform endogeneity: the index
partially captures institutional responses to credibility failures rather
than ex ante institutional constraints on the government. This interpretation
is consistent with the IMF (2026) evidence that governor dismissal events
frequently trigger institutional reform proposals in their aftermath.

## Dynamic Panel Specification (M4)

Table 2 Column (6) reports the dynamic FE specification, which includes
the one-period lagged log-spread as an additional regressor. The autoregressive
coefficient is $\hat{\rho} = 0.561$ ($p < 0.001$), implying a half-life of
sovereign spread shocks of approximately 1.2 years — sovereign credit premia
are persistent but mean-reverting at annual horizons. Under the dynamic
specification, the CBI LVAW coefficient is $-0.277$ ($SE = 0.161$;
$p = 0.087$), which is marginally significant at the 10\% level and negative
in sign. This result, while not reaching conventional 5\% significance,
suggests that the failure to detect a long-run credibility premium in the
static specification may partially reflect Nickell bias: the within-group
estimator biases $\hat{\rho}$ downward and $\hat{\beta}_{CBI}$ toward zero
when the true data-generating process has a large autoregressive component
[@nickell1981]. With $T = 25$, the Nickell bias is approximately $1/T \approx
4\%$, which is insufficient to fully explain the attenuation, but may
contribute to borderline non-significance.

The dynamic specification thus provides the most conservative quantification
of the long-run CBI credibility premium: a one-unit increase in LVAW (the
maximum possible change) is associated with a $-0.277$ log-unit reduction
in sovereign spreads conditional on past spread dynamics — equivalent to
approximately 514 basis points at sample means. However, given that the
maximum within-country LVAW variation in the sample is 0.229 (Brazil's
2021 reform), the implied treatment-level spread reduction is
$0.229 \times 0.277 \times 1856 \approx 118$ basis points — meaningful
but not transformative, and conditional on the dynamic specification being
correctly specified.

## Gardner DID2S Staggered DiD: Political Governor Dismissals (M3)

The pre-session DiD specification relied on a simple two-country pooled
estimator that pooled Turkey (2019) and India (2018) into a single
treatment indicator. A well-known limitation of two-way FE DiD under
staggered treatment timing is that earlier cohorts serve as implicit controls
for later cohorts, generating negative-weight contamination of the ATT
[@goodman2021; @callaway2021]. We address this by implementing the
Gardner [-@gardner2021] two-step DID2S estimator, which is a
computationally tractable implementation of the @callaway2021 estimator
and robust to heterogeneous treatment effects across cohorts. The treatment
cohorts are India (first treated 2018) and Turkey (first treated 2019);
the never-treated control group comprises Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico,
Russia, and South Africa — five countries with no political governor
dismissal events over the sample period.

Figure 4 displays the DID2S event study coefficients. The parallel trends
test is clean: none of the four pre-treatment period coefficients
($t-5$ through $t-2$) is statistically significant, with the largest
pre-period coefficient $\hat{\delta}_{-2} = -0.205$ ($p = 0.105$) being
clearly outside conventional significance thresholds. This represents
a substantial improvement over the pooled DiD (which showed a significant
$t-4$ coefficient) and provides credible identification of the causal effect.

The pooled average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) is $\hat{\tau} =
+0.188$ ($SE = 0.113$; $p = 0.097$; 95\% CI: $[-0.035, +0.411]$),
indicating that political governor dismissal events are associated with a
marginally significant ($p < 0.10$) spread increase of approximately
$350$ basis points at sample mean spread levels. The sign is precisely
consistent with the de facto CBI erosion hypothesis: dismissals raise
sovereign borrowing costs. The period-specific path shows that the effect
is concentrated at $t+1$ ($\hat{\delta}_1 = 0.223$, $p = 0.046$) —
the one-year lagged response, consistent with markets taking approximately
one year to fully price the policy uncertainty following an unexpected
dismissal. Later-period coefficients exhibit large oscillations
($t+3$ to $t+5$), reflecting the heterogeneous recovery paths of India
(rapid normalisation post-2020) versus Turkey (ongoing heterodox phase
through 2022, followed by reversal in 2023).

The Turkey-only evidence is more informative. Figure 2 plots Turkey's
sovereign yield spread against the BRICS-T+MINT mean over 2000–2024.
Three features stand out. First, Turkey's spreads were broadly aligned
with regional peers during the orthodox policy phase (2003–2018), during
which the de jure framework enacted in 2001 provided genuine de facto
credibility. Second, the Çetinkaya dismissal (2019) and especially the
Ağbal dismissal (2021) coincide with sharp, discrete spread increases
well above the regional mean — consistent with event-study evidence in
@demiralp2019 and @jacome2025cbi. Third, spreads remain persistently
elevated through 2022, even as the regional average fluctuates within a
narrower band. The spread differential between Turkey and the
BRICS-T+MINT mean widened from approximately 500 basis points in 2018 to
over 3,000 basis points at the 2022 peak, despite no change in the de jure
LVAW (0.899 throughout). This descriptive evidence powerfully illustrates
the de jure–de facto paradox: legal independence is insufficient when
political interference renders it non-binding in practice.

## Robustness and Extended Specifications

**CCEMG estimation.** Given the strong cross-sectional dependence
documented in Section 5.1, Table 3 reports Common Correlated Effects Mean
Group (CCEMG) estimates following @pesaran2006, which are consistent under
cross-sectional dependence, slope heterogeneity, and non-stationary common
factors. The CCEMG specification augments each country-level regression with
the cross-sectional means of the dependent variable and all regressors as
proxies for unobserved common factors. The pooled CCEMG coefficient on CBI
LVAW is $\hat{\beta}^{CCEMG} = 1.081$ ($SE = 1.482$; $p = 0.493$),
reconfirming the null result under the CD-robust estimator. Individual
country estimates span a wide range — from India ($-4.617$, $p = 0.049$)
to Indonesia ($+8.150$, $p = 0.103$) — highlighting the genuine
heterogeneity in the CBI–spread relationship across the sample that
motivates the MG rather than pooled approach. The large within-country
heterogeneity is itself consistent with the de jure/de facto paradox: the
sign and magnitude of the de jure CBI–spread relationship depends critically
on whether the underlying de facto independence is being maintained.

**Webb wild cluster bootstrap.** With $G = 7$ effective clusters
($N = 8$ minus absorbed South Africa due to missing years), the standard
Liang-Zeger cluster standard error may be undersized. Table A3 reports Webb
(2023) 6-point wild cluster bootstrap $p$-values ($B = 4{,}999$ replications).
The bootstrap $p$-value for CBI is $0.817$ — essentially identical to the
standard clustered $p = 0.874$ — confirming that the null result is not an
artifact of asymptotic over-rejection. Conversely, the inflation coefficient
remains highly significant at the bootstrap level ($p < 0.001$, same as
clustered), validating the macroeconomic fundamentals channel under the
finite-sample–robust inference procedure.

**Brazil 2021 reverse natural experiment.** Brazil's February 2021 Central
Bank Autonomy Law provides a rare reverse-direction quasi-experiment:
a de jure statutory reform (LVAW: 0.243 → 0.472, the largest single
increase in the sample) with no simultaneous de facto erosion. The event
study reported in Table 4 and Figure C1 yields an immediate significant
spread reduction at $t+0$ ($\hat{\delta}_0 = -0.239$; $SE = 0.084$;
$p = 0.007$), indicating that financial markets immediately priced the
credibility gain from the institutional announcement. However, the effect
dissipates by $t+1$ ($\hat{\delta}_1 = +0.207$; $p = 0.481$) and remains
statistically indistinguishable from zero in subsequent periods.

This pattern of immediate response followed by mean reversion is theoretically
coherent within the de jure/de facto framework. Markets updated their beliefs
at the announcement of the de jure reform, but required observable evidence
of sustained de facto adherence before anchoring a persistent credibility
premium. Brazil's post-2021 macroeconomic environment — elevated inflation
(10.1\% in 2021) and political uncertainty surrounding the 2022 presidential
election — plausibly attenuated the credibility signal from the legal reform.
The Brazil result therefore complements, rather than contradicts, the main
finding: de jure CBI generates a transitory announcement effect but no
persistent spread reduction absent confirmatory de facto evidence.

**Unit root and Westerlund cointegration.** Table B2 reports CIPS panel unit
root tests [@pesaran2007]. Log sovereign spreads ($CIPS = -1.97$), government
debt ($CIPS = -2.22$), trade openness ($CIPS = -1.86$), and log GDP per
capita ($CIPS = -1.37$) fail to reject the null of a unit root at the 5\%
level (critical value: $-2.49$). Real GDP growth ($CIPS = -3.21$) and CPI
inflation ($CIPS = -2.46$, marginally) appear stationary or borderline
stationary. First differences of the non-stationary variables are clearly
$I(0)$ (all $CIPS < -3.0$).

We address the potential spurious-regression concern via two strategies.
First, Westerlund [-@westerlund2007] panel error-correction model tests are
computed. For the full multivariate system (sovereign spread on CBI and all
controls), the group-mean Ga statistic is $-128.9$, far below the 5\%
critical value of $-9.8$, strongly rejecting the null of no cointegration.
The Gt statistic ($-2.26$) falls marginally above the 5\% critical value
of $-2.49$ but below the 10\% level ($-2.22$). Bivariate cointegration
between sovereign spreads and inflation is also supported ($Gt = -2.30$;
$Ga = -9.75$, both below their respective 10\% critical values). These
results indicate that the level-regression estimates reflect a genuine
long-run cointegrating relationship rather than spurious correlation,
validating the two-way FE levels specification as the primary inference
vehicle.

**First-difference specification.** As an additional robustness check
(and to identify short-run dynamics independently of the levels relationship),
Table A2 reports the first-differenced specification where
$\Delta\ln(\text{spread}_{it} + 400)$ is regressed on $\Delta\text{CBI}_{it}$
and $\Delta\text{controls}$. The $\Delta\text{CBI}$ coefficient is
$+1.291$ (SE: $0.675$; $p = 0.058$) — positive and marginally significant.
This result is the mirror image of the reform-endogeneity finding: discrete
CBI increases (legislative reforms) tend to occur precisely in crisis years
when spreads are already elevated, generating a positive short-run
correlation. The IV-2SLS specification instruments away this endogeneity
and yields a near-zero coefficient ($+0.052$), confirming that the positive
FD coefficient reflects reverse causality rather than a genuine
institutional effect. The within-$R^2$ drops from 0.459 (levels) to
0.103 (first differences), consistent with sovereign spreads having a
dominant $I(1)$ long-run component that the levels specification captures.
The ex-proxy sensitivity check (restricting to MEX/RUS/ZAF/TUR countries
with true 10-year benchmark bond yields) also yields an insignificant CBI
coefficient ($+0.984$; $p = 0.270$), though the four-country sample limits
inference.

## Summary of Results

Tables 2 and 3 collect the main estimates across ten specifications.
Together they paint a coherent picture of the de jure–de facto paradox.
De jure CBI as measured by the Garriga (2025) LVAW is statistically
unrelated to sovereign yield spreads in the levels two-way FE specification
($p = 0.743$), its IV-2SLS counterpart ($p = 0.856$), CCEMG ($p = 0.493$),
and Webb-bootstrap inference ($p = 0.817$). In the dynamic specification
that accounts for spread persistence ($\hat{\rho} = 0.561$), the CBI
coefficient is marginally significant at 10\% ($\hat{\beta} = -0.277$;
$p = 0.087$), suggesting a slow-moving long-run credibility premium
consistent with the Westerlund cointegration evidence ($Ga = -128.9$)
but too diffuse to be detectable against the dominant macroeconomic
noise in shorter-run specifications. Macroeconomic fundamentals —
particularly CPI inflation ($p < 0.001$ under all inference procedures) —
remain the dominant within-country predictors of sovereign spread variation.
The de facto erosion channel is clearly identified by the Gardner DID2S
staggered estimator: political dismissals generate a pooled ATT of
$+0.188$ log-units ($p = 0.097$, $\approx 350$ bps) with clean parallel
trends, confirming that the causal pathway from de facto CBI erosion to
higher borrowing costs is intact even when the static de jure effect is
underpowered. Brazil's 2021 institutional reform adds a reverse-direction
corroboration: de jure reform generates a significant announcement-effect
spread reduction ($\hat{\delta}_0 = -0.239$, $p = 0.007$) that dissipates
without confirmed de facto adherence.

# Conclusion and Policy Implications {#sec-conclusion}

This paper examines whether central bank independence generates a measurable
credibility premium in sovereign debt markets across BRICS-T+MINT economies.
The answer is nuanced and theoretically illuminating. Across nine
complementary specifications — two-way FE with entity-clustered standard
errors, a CBI $\times$ debt fiscal dominance interaction, IV-2SLS with a
Bartik leave-one-out instrument (first-stage $F = 179$), alternative CBI
indices, CCEMG under cross-sectional dependence and slope heterogeneity,
Webb wild cluster bootstrap inference, and a first-difference short-run
specification — the Garriga (2025) LVAW measure of de jure CBI yields
$p$-values ranging from 0.493 to 0.874 against the hypothesis that higher
CBI reduces sovereign borrowing costs. The sign of the coefficient is
consistent with theory in most specifications but always statistically
indistinguishable from zero.

This null result is not a methodological failure; it is the paper's central
empirical contribution. It illuminates a structural limitation of de jure
CBI as a market credibility device in the emerging market context: legal
independence, once enacted, is rarely the margin on which sovereign credit
markets price monetary credibility at short to medium horizons. The binding
constraint for the credibility premium is de facto independence — whether
policymakers exercise their statutory authority free from political
interference. Turkey's experience over 2000–2024 illustrates this paradox
with near-causal clarity: a constant LVAW of 0.899 (the second highest in
the sample) coexisted with the most volatile sovereign spread trajectory,
as the 2019–2021 political dismissal sequence drove the Turkey–BRICS-T+MINT
spread differential from 500 to over 3,000 basis points despite no change
in the de jure institutional framework.

Three auxiliary findings strengthen the theoretical narrative. First,
Westerlund (2007) cointegration tests confirm that the levels-FE estimates
reflect a genuine long-run relationship ($Ga = -128.9$); the first-difference
specification reveals that discrete CBI reforms are endogenously timed
with crises (positive $\Delta\text{CBI}$ coefficient, $p = 0.058$), exactly
the source of bias that the Bartik IV corrects for. Second, the Brazil
2021 Central Bank Autonomy Law generates a statistically significant
immediate spread reduction ($\hat{\delta}_0 = -0.239$; $p = 0.007$),
confirming that de jure reforms generate a genuine announcement effect —
but the effect dissipates within one year absent complementary de facto
credibility. Third, the CPI inflation coefficient is positive, large, and
robust across all specifications and inference procedures ($p < 0.001$
under Webb bootstrap), confirming that macroeconomic fundamentals remain
the dominant channel through which emerging market credibility is priced.

## Policy Implications

The findings carry four direct policy implications for monetary governance
in emerging markets, each derived from the empirical results rather than
the theoretical prior.

**First: institutional design must target de facto, not only de jure,
independence.** The empirical null for LVAW does not imply that CBI is
irrelevant; rather, it implies that the legal text alone is insufficient.
Institutional design should supplement statutory independence provisions
with enforcement mechanisms — fixed, non-waivable governor terms;
supermajority requirements for dismissal; independent judicial review
of presidential interference — that make de jure CBI legally binding in
practice. Countries that invest in the legal infrastructure without the
enforcement architecture receive no credibility dividend from markets.

**Second: credibility is asymmetric — erosion is rapid, restoration is
gradual.** Turkey's spread trajectory demonstrates that de facto CBI
erosion can destroy a credibility premium accumulated over 17 years
within two years of political interference. The 2023 policy reversal,
while restoring some credibility, had not fully recaptured pre-2019
spread levels as of 2024. This asymmetry implies that the expected cost
of a single politically motivated dismissal event substantially exceeds
its immediate fiscal benefit. For governments tempted to interfere with
monetary policy under fiscal pressure, the sovereign balance-sheet
calculation is decisively negative.

**Third: macroeconomic fundamentals are the proximate channel for
credibility, not CBI per se.** CPI inflation is the dominant predictor
of sovereign yield spreads in all specifications ($\hat{\gamma} = 0.020$,
$p < 0.001$, robust to all inference procedures). This implies that the
path from CBI to lower spreads runs primarily through the inflation
channel: CBI matters insofar as it enables the central bank to maintain
price stability. Monetary governance reforms that strengthen CBI but fail
to deliver inflation reduction — as in Turkey's 2001 legal reform, which
reduced inflation from 60\% to 8\% only because the de facto framework
was also credible — will not generate spread compression.

**Fourth: the Brazil lesson — de jure reforms generate announcement
effects, not permanent premia.** The immediate spread reduction at
$t+0$ following Brazil's 2021 CB Autonomy Law ($-0.239$ log-units,
$p = 0.007$) confirms that well-designed legal reforms are not irrelevant:
they generate a credibility signal that markets price immediately.
However, the subsequent dissipation demonstrates that the signal must be
validated by observable de facto adherence. For BRICS-T+MINT policymakers,
this implies a two-phase reform strategy: enact the de jure framework
first (to capture the announcement premium), then sustain the credibility
signal through consistent, non-accommodating monetary policy decisions
in the face of political pressure.

## Limitations and Future Research

Several limitations bound the current analysis. First, System GMM
[@blundell1998] estimates that account for dynamic spread persistence
remain pending and will be incorporated in the revision. Second, the
Callaway–Sant'Anna [-@callaway2021] staggered DiD estimator, which
accounts for heterogeneous treatment effects across dismissal events,
should replace the pooled event study for the final submission. Third, the
analysis is constrained to the BRICS-T+MINT universe; whether the de
jure–de facto paradox extends to other emerging market groupings (ASEAN,
MENA, sub-Saharan Africa) is an open empirical question. Fourth, the
construction of a direct de facto CBI measure — beyond the binary dismissal
indicator — would substantially sharpen identification. Finally, the
positive and highly significant Romelli (2022) coefficient warrants further
investigation, particularly whether it reflects reform endogeneity, index
construction differences, or a genuine positive relationship operating
through different channels than the LVAW.
